steps.description: Implement a controlled numerical experiment to test the geometric hypothesis on solution-space rigidity using small feedforward networks. The script will: (1) Define a constraint function f(x) with known analytic properties; (2) Generate w training samples; (3) Train networks with varying hidden widths N; (4) Measure max absolute error on a held-out validation set; (5) Determine N_c(w) as the minimal width achieving zero violation (error ≤ 1e-3). The experiment will sweep w from 5 to 50 and N from 2 to 100, logging training/validation errors and N_c values. Results will be analyzed for rigidity (finite N_c constant in w) vs. fatness (N_c diverges or is unattainable).

Design and execute a numerical experiment to test the "geometry" hypothesis regarding solution space rigidity in small feedforward networks. Specifically: (1) define a family of analytic constraints (e.g., polynomial or trigonometric functions with known smoothness); (2) sample w constraint points; (3) sweep hidden layer width N from 4 to 64; (4) train network to minimize loss on training set; (5) evaluate max absolute error on held-out validation set; (6) record N_c(w) as minimum width achieving zero violation (error ≤ 1e-3); (7) repeat for multiple w values to assess scaling. Use standard activation (ReLU/Tanh), Adam optimizer, and sufficient training iterations to convergence. Plot N_c(w) vs w and assess whether N_c remains bounded (rigid) or grows unbounded (fat). Validate against literature on neural network capacity and Kolmogorov width.

Design a bootstrap experiment to probe solution space rigidity of small feedforward networks. Generate an analytic constraint function (e.g., a polynomial or trigonometric function) with known properties. Sweep constraint sample size w and hidden layer width N. For each (w, N) pair, train a small feedforward network on w points, evaluate maximum absolute error on a held-out test set of constraints. Record N_c(w) = minimum N achieving max error ≤ 1e3. Plot N_c vs w to determine if rigidity (bounded N_c) holds. Use fixed random seeds for reproducibility.

plans.objective: [DIM: optimization] The minimal network capacity N_c(w) follows a phase-transition scaling: for w < w_c (critical constraint density), N_c(w) remains constant (rigid regime), while for w > w_c, N_c(w) diverges exponentially with w (fat regime), reflecting a sharp transition in solution space accessibility.

steps.description: Implement a numerical experiment to test the phase-transition scaling hypothesis for minimal network capacity N_c(w) as a function of constraint density w. The experiment will: (1) Define a bootstrap constraint problem using a target function with known analytical constraints; (2) Systematically vary w (constraint count) and N (hidden layer width); (3) Train small feedforward networks to satisfy constraints; (4) Measure N_c(w) as the minimum width achieving zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out constraints; (5) Analyze scaling behavior to identify rigid vs. fat regimes and critical w_c. The code will generate the required scan data, training/validation metrics, and N_c(w) values for analysis.

plans.objective: [DIM: Optimization] The learning dynamics induce a phase transition in solution space accessibility: for $w$ below a critical density, the optimization landscape allows a solution at a fixed minimal width $N_{crit}$, independent of $w$, due to the existence of a broad basin of attraction that accommodates increasing constraints without widening the solution manifold.

steps.description: Perform a systematic scan of constraint density w (10 to 200) and network width N (8 to 256) to determine N_c(w). For each w, train small feedforward networks on w randomly generated constraints (e.g., polynomial or trigonometric functions with known analytical forms), then evaluate the maximum absolute error on a held-out set of constraints. Identify the minimal N that achieves zero violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3) for each w. Analyze the scaling behavior: if N_c(w) saturates at a finite value below w_c, this supports the phase transition hypothesis; if N_c(w) grows or remains unbounded, the solution space is "fat". Use PyTorch for training, Adam optimizer, and ensure convergence via validation loss plateauing. Validate results against the baseline from iteration 20 (surprise=1.0) to identify discrepancies in the critical density or saturation behavior.

Design and execute a bootstrap experiment to test if small feedforward networks act as probes of solution space rigidity. Define a target function family of 2D polynomial constraints $f(x,y) = \sum_{i=0}^d \sum_{j=0}^d c_{ij} x^i y^j$ with degree $d=4$ and constraint density $w$ defined as the ratio of constraint points to input dimensions ($w = N_{pts}/2$). Train small feedforward networks with hidden width $N \in [8, 256]$ and measure $N_c(w)$ — the minimum width achieving max absolute error $\le 10^{-3}$ on held-out constraints. Scan $w \in [10, 200]$ to observe if $N_c$ remains bounded (rigid) or diverges (fat). Use symbolic regression on the recovered solution to identify functional form, validating against the ground-truth polynomial.

We will test the Algebraic Rank Hypothesis by numerically measuring the solution space rigidity of small MLPs. We will: (1) generate a synthetic constraint set (e.g., a smooth target function with w evaluation points); (2) train small MLPs of increasing hidden width N_c on w constraints; (3) measure the maximum absolute error on a held-out set of constraints; (4) define N_c(w) as the smallest width achieving zero violation (max error ≤ 1e-3); (5) scan w to observe if N_c(w) remains bounded (rigid) or diverges (fat). This directly probes whether bootstrap solution space rigidity is detectable via MLP generalization.

plans.objective: [DIM: STRUCTURE] The minimal network capacity $N_c(w)$ is determined by the rank of the constraint matrix in the dual space; for algebraically structured constraints (e.g., polynomial identities), $N_c(w)$ scales linearly with the rank $r$ of the constraint matrix, independent of $w$ beyond a saturation point. | predict: $N_c(w) = \min(r, w)$ where $r$ is the rank of the dual constraint matrix; for $w \geq r$, $N_c(w)$ plateaus at $r$. | pro: Directly links network capacity to algebraic structure of constraints, testable via rank analysis. con: Requires explicit constraint matrix construction, may not capture nonlinear interactions in neural networks.

steps.description: Reformulate the hypothesis to test the rigidity of the solution space rather than interpolation capacity. We will generate polynomial identity constraints with a known dual constraint matrix rank $r$, train a network with width $w$, and measure the dimension of the solution space (number of free parameters after constraints) as a function of $w$. The prediction is that for $w \geq r$, the solution space dimension saturates, indicating algebraic rigidity independent of further width increase. This avoids the interpolation contradiction by measuring structural capacity rather than fitting error.

plans.objective: [STRUCTURE] The minimal network capacity N_c(w) is determined by the rank of the constraint matrix in the dual space; for algebraically structured constraints, N_c(w) saturates at a constant value equal to the intrinsic dimensionality of the constraint manifold, independent of w beyond a threshold.

[STRUCTURE] Algebraic Rank Saturation. The minimal network capacity $N_c(w)$ remains constant (rigid) as the number of constraints $w$ increases, provided the constraints lie within a subspace of dimension bounded by the network's expressive power. Once the number of independent constraints exceeds the subspace dimension, $N_c$ must increase abruptly or zero-violation becomes impossible. This predicts a step-function-like behavior in $N_c(w)$, distinct from the logarithmic scaling of the Measure hypothesis or the linear scaling of the Complexity hypothesis.

steps.description: We will test the Algebraic Rank Saturation hypothesis by numerically scanning the minimal network capacity N_c(w) as a function of constraint count w. The plan involves: (1) generating synthetic constraint functions with known algebraic structure (polynomials/sinusoids) to control the subspace dimension; (2) training small feedforward networks of varying hidden widths; (3) measuring the minimum width required to achieve zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out constraints; (4) plotting N_c(w) to detect step-function saturation versus logarithmic/linear scaling. This directly addresses the core assertion that N_c remains rigid until constraints exceed subspace dimension.
